lead: The second week of the Season of the Apostles opens with two readings about the future God has prepared for our bodies. Paul tells the Philippians that their citizenship is in heaven and that Christ will transform the body of our humiliation to be like his glorious body. At Bethany, Jesus tells a grieving Martha, “I am the resurrection and the life,” and she answers with a full confession of faith.

set: Paul writes to the Philippians from prison; where he was held, whether in Rome, Ephesus or Caesarea, is still debated. Philippi was a Roman colony (Acts 16:12), and its people were proud to be citizens of Rome, far away. In chapter 3 Paul has warned against those who insisted on circumcision for Gentile believers, and he has told of counting all things loss for Christ (3:7–8). Now he warns against another danger: a life governed by appetite.
str: v. 16: hold fast to what you have attained.
v. 17: imitate me, and watch those who live by our example.
vv. 18–19: with tears: enemies of the cross, whose god is the belly.
vv. 20–21: our citizenship is in heaven; the Saviour will transform our bodies.
kw: The word the people of a Roman colony would have used of their belonging to Rome. Christians belong to a homeland in heaven, and they live in this world as its citizens.
“Their god is the belly” describes people ruled by their appetites. Scholars debate whom Paul has in mind; what is clear is that he warns of a life without the cross.
The same root as in 3:10, “becoming like him in his death”. Those who share the form of Christ’s cross will share the form of his glory.
vv: Brothers and sisters, join in imitating me, and observe those who live according to the example you have in us.
Paul is not proud; he has just said he has not yet reached the goal (3:12). He offers himself as a model of one who runs toward Christ. Faith is learned by watching faithful people.
For many live as enemies of the cross of Christ; I have often told you of them, and now I tell you even with tears.
Paul’s warning comes with tears, not anger. He weeps for those who reject the cross.
But our citizenship is in heaven, and it is from there that we are expecting a Savior, the Lord Jesus Christ.
In the Roman world “saviour” and “lord” were titles given to the emperor. Paul gives them to Jesus, who will come not from Rome but from heaven.
He will transform the body of our humiliation that it may be conformed to the body of his glory,
Not a “vile body”, as older translations put it, but a lowly body, weak and mortal. God does not throw away our bodies; he will glorify them.
ch: The early Letter to Diognetus describes Christians in Paul’s spirit: they live on earth, but they are citizens of heaven, and they obey the laws while surpassing them by their lives. The Catechism teaches that in the resurrection Christ will raise our bodies, transformed into the likeness of his glorious body (CCC 999–1000). The hope of heaven does not take us out of the world; the Second Vatican Council teaches that it should rather urge us to work for a better earth (Gaudium et Spes 39).

r.h: I am the resurrection and the life
set: Lazarus of Bethany, the brother of Martha and Mary, was a friend Jesus loved (11:3, 5). Jesus delayed two days before going to Judea, where his life was in danger (11:6–8). Bethany was a village on the Mount of Olives, about three kilometres from Jerusalem; the Greek says fifteen stadia. The raising of Lazarus is the seventh and greatest of the signs in John’s Gospel, and it leads the authorities to resolve to put Jesus to death (11:53).

The “Jews” who had come to console the sisters are their neighbours and friends from Jerusalem, carrying out the work of mercy of comforting mourners. In this chapter many of them come to believe (11:45).
str: vv. 17–19: four days in the tomb; many come to console.
vv. 20–22: Martha goes to meet Jesus: “Lord, if you had been here.”
vv. 23–24: “Your brother will rise again”; “on the last day”.
vv. 25–26: “I am the resurrection and the life… Do you believe this?”
v. 27: Martha’s confession: the Messiah, the Son of God.
kw: Lazarus has been dead four days. A later Jewish tradition held that the soul stayed near the body for three days; after four days death was beyond doubt. The sign will be undeniable.

Martha believes in the resurrection of the dead at the last day, as many Jews of her time did, especially the Pharisees (Acts 23:8). Jesus brings that hope into the present: the resurrection is a person, and he is here.
The fifth of the seven “I am” sayings with an image in John (bread, light, gate, shepherd, resurrection, way, vine). It echoes the name of God revealed to Moses (Exodus 3:14).
vv: When Jesus arrived, he found that Lazarus had already been in the tomb four days.
Jesus seems to arrive too late. In John, God’s timing is never late; it serves a greater sign (11:4).
Lord, if you had been here, my brother would not have died.
Martha speaks with the honesty of a friend. Her grief and her faith stand side by side, and Jesus does not rebuke her.
Jesus said to her, “I am the resurrection and the life. Those who believe in me, even though they die, will live,

Textual note: a few early witnesses, among them a papyrus of the third century, lack the words “and the life”. Nearly all manuscripts have them, and the Church reads them. Those who believe will die in body, yet live; and those who live in him will never die the death that separates from God.
Yes, Lord, I believe that you are the Messiah, the Son of God, the one coming into the world.
Martha’s confession is as full as Peter’s at Caesarea Philippi (Matthew 16:16). It is almost the very confession for which John wrote his Gospel (20:31).
ch: The Catechism quotes this verse when it teaches that Jesus links faith in the resurrection to his own person: “I am the resurrection and the life” (CCC 994). The Church reads this Gospel at funerals and prays in her liturgy that for the faithful life is changed, not ended. Martha, often remembered for being busy (Luke 10:40), is here the one who makes the great confession; the Church honours Martha, Mary and Lazarus together as saints (29 July in the Roman calendar).

qa: If Jesus is the resurrection, why do believers still die?

Jesus does not promise that believers will escape bodily death; Lazarus himself would die again. He promises that death no longer has the last word: those who believe in him, “even though they die, will live”. The Catechism teaches that for those who die in Christ’s grace, death is a participation in his death, so that they may also share his Resurrection (CCC 1006, 1010).
study: Paul says, “our citizenship is in heaven.” In what everyday choices does my true homeland show?
Martha brought both her grief and her faith to Jesus. What sorrow do I need to bring to him honestly today?
